faq.q: Can a patient have both obstructive and restrictive patterns?

faq.a: Give supplemental oxygen to keep SpO₂ 88‑92%, start short‑acting bronchodilator, and assess for infection.

exam: A 55‑year‑old farmer with chronic cough presents with worsening dyspnoea; spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.62 and FEV1 55% pred. – Identify severity and immediate management steps.
A 30‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with dry cough and restrictive spirometry (FVC 58% pred, ratio 0.78). – List likely causes and the key investigation to confirm.

ai.title: Obstructive versus Restrictive Lung Disease
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Obstructive and restrictive lung diseases produce opposite patterns on spirometry and have distinct clinical clues. Recognising the pattern guides diagnosis, severity staging, and management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Obstructive: FEV1/FVC <0.70, often with reduced FEV1.
sections.p: Obstructive disease limits airflow out of the lungs (low FEV1/FVC <0.70); restrictive disease limits lung expansion (normal or high FEV1/FVC with reduced FVC). Spirometry is the cornerstone.

t.b: Is the pattern obstructive or restrictive? → Ratio <0.70 = obstructive; ratio ≥0.70 with low FVC = restrictive.

b: Obstructive (COPD) GOLD 1–4 based on post‑bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted.
sections.p: Obstructive disease severity uses GOLD (COPD) or asthma control categories; restrictive disease uses % predicted FVC and clinical impact.

b: Obstructive: chronic biomass smoke exposure, tobacco, post‑TB bronchiectasis, HIV‑related chronic bronchitis.
Restrictive: pulmonary TB scarring, post‑pneumonia fibrosis, silicosis (mining), sarcoidosis, HIV‑associated interstitial lung disease.
sections.p: Identify the most common aetiologies in low‑resource East African settings before rarer causes.

b: Obstructive: progressive dyspnoea, chronic cough with sputum, wheeze, barrel chest, prolonged expiratory phase.
Restrictive: early dyspnoea on exertion, dry cough, tachypnoea, reduced chest expansion, fine crackles.
sections.p: History and exam differentiate the two patterns.
Use available tests wisely; when a test is missing, rely on clinical clues.

t.b: What structural pattern is present? → Hyperinflation in obstruction; reduced lung volumes, fibrosis, or pleural thickening in restriction.
Is the patient hypoxic? → SpO2 <90% warrants supplemental O₂.
Is there hypercapnia or hypoxaemia? → Elevated PaCO₂ suggests advanced obstruction; low PaO₂ common to both.
What is the pattern of parenchymal disease? → Emphysema bullae vs. fibrotic bands.

b: Obstructive: acute exacerbation with worsening dyspnoea, sputum change, fever, PaO₂ <80 mmHg, or rising PaCO₂.
Restrictive: rapid progression of fibrosis, development of cor pulmonale, severe hypoxaemia.
sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that need urgent action.

b: Obstructive: smoking/biomass cessation, bronchodilators (β2‑agonist, anticholinergic), inhaled steroids for asthma, antibiotics for infection, pulmonary rehab.
Restrictive: treat infection (TB therapy), steroids for inflammatory fibrosis, antifibrotics where available, oxygen for chronic hypoxaemia.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide symptom‑based therapy.

b: Obstructive: repeat spirometry every 6–12 months, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), educate on inhaler technique.
Restrictive: monitor FVC, screen for O₂ requirement, counsel on avoiding dust exposure.
sections.p: Regular review of lung function and risk‑factor control reduces progression.

b: Obstructive: asthma vs. COPD; bronchiectasis vs. chronic bronchitis.
Restrictive: pleural effusion (low volumes) vs. true parenchymal restriction.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic the clinical picture.

b: Obstructive: early disease may have normal FEV1/FVC if effort is poor; bronchodilator response can be blunted in severe COPD.
Restrictive: obesity can lower FVC without true parenchymal disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness with chest tightness or cyanosis
